Definition. If a and fi are real numbers, then
a + fi = {x : x = y + z for some y in a and some z in fi}.
theorem If a and fi are real numbers, then a + fi is a real number.
proof Once again four facts must be verified.
(1) Suppose w < x for some x in a + fi. Then x = y + z for some yin ot and
some z in fi, which means that w < y + z, and consequently, w— y < z.
This shows that w — y is in fi (since zis in fi,and fi is a real number). Since
w = y + (w — y), it follows that w is in a + fi.
(2) It is clear that a + fi 0, since a 0 and fi fi 0.

not in ci and b not in fi. Any x in a satisfies x < a (for if a < x, then

shows that a + b is not in a + fi, so a + fi fi Q.
(4) If x is in a + fi, then x = y + z for y in a and z in fi. There are y' in a
and z' in fi with y < y' and z < zf then x < y' + z' and y' + z' is in a + fi.
Thus a + fi has no greatest member. |
By now you can see how tiresome this whole procedure is going to be. Every time
we mention a new real number, we must prove that it is a real number; this requires
checking four conditions, and even when trivial they require concentration. There
is really no help for this (except that it will be less boring if you check the four
conditions for yourself). Fortunately, however, a few points of interest will arise
now and then, and some of our theorems will be easy. In particular, two properties
of + present no problems.

of (a + fi) + y is also a member of a + (fi + y), and vice versa. |
